en: The *Commentary on the Proof of Consciousness-Only*, Volume Seventeen, states that this stage is subsumed within [the path of preparation].
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* explains that the stages prior to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are called the "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

To distinguish them from those of the two vehicles, it specifies "Mahāyāna. Second, the stage of application (*prayoga*) is contained within the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), such as Heat and the others. This...

The first two belong to the initial stage (*ādikarmika*). The third is the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*), which occurs at the very beginning of the first bhūmi, within the initial moment of entering that bhūmi.

The fourth is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), beginning from the second moment of mind in the first bhūmi up to the stage of the vajra-mind; this is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The fifth is the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā*), which, following the vajra-mind, exists throughout the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) until the end of the future.
These are included within these five stages, which will be explained in the subsequent text.
"How does one gradually awaken to and enter into consciousness-only?
This interrogates the third section.
This means that bodhisattvas, during the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), are able to develop profound faith and understanding regarding the characteristics and nature of consciousness;

in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), they are able to gradually suppress and eliminate the grasped object and the grasping subject, thereby eliciting true vision; and in the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), they penetrate reality as it truly is.

In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), one repeatedly practices according to the principles as they have been perceived, thereby subduing and severing the obstacles until reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*).

Having emerged from these obstacles, one becomes perfectly luminous and is able to transform sentient beings throughout the future; furthermore, one causes them to awaken to and enter into the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

The first two lines apply generally to all subsequent stages. This stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is not merely one of faith and understanding; it is also capable of suppressing and eliminating [afflictions].

However, because these have not yet been extensively removed, they are omitted from the description. Within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), one first suppresses the grasped object (*grāhya*) and subsequently suppresses the grasping subject (*grāhaka*);
this suppression, such that they do not arise, is termed "elimination. It is only in the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*) that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom actually arises.
By practicing the two wisdoms, one realizes the nature of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) and penetrates it as it truly is.

During the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), one practices moment by moment according to the principle thus realized, subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*) and severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Upon reaching the ultimate stage, one completely emerges from the two obstructions;

this is termed "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*) because it differs from that of the Lesser Vehicle sages. Furthermore, because its merit and wisdom are purified, it is named [the Buddha-fruit], as it differs from that of the Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of illumination, and continuing until the end of the future, he transforms classes of sentient beings, enabling others to realize the characteristics and nature of consciousness.
What are the characteristics of the initial stage of the equipment (sambhāra-avasthā)?
A separate explanation of the five stages is divided into five parts. This explains the first stage; it is a general inquiry that introduces the topic.
The verse says:
"Until consciousness has yet arisen, one seeks to abide in the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*); regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two graspings,"
Why has this not yet been subdued and extinguished?
[The author] answers by citing a verse. Since it is explained in the prose commentary (*dīrghapaṅkti*), it is not clarified here in advance.

The treatise says: From the generation of the profound and firm mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) until the consciousness that accords with the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-vijñāna*) has not yet arisen, one seeks to abide...
The true ultimate nature of consciousness-only—up to this point, all are subsumed within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

This is because one accumulates various superior provisions for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and because, for the sake of sentient beings, one diligently seeks liberation.
For these reasons, it is also called the "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

The commentary explains the first two lines of the verse: from the initial generation of the bodhicitta at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), up until the arising of the consciousness that accords with the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-vijñāna*).

As for the "consciousness that accords with the stage of penetration," this refers to the consciousness of the stage of penetration; it means that the consciousness of this stage performs the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra-darśana*).

One seeks to abide in consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). At this stage, one has not yet been able to suppress or eliminate the marks of consciousness (*vijñapti-nimitta*); thus, it is not yet called "seeking to abide in the true nature of consciousness-only.
All forty stages of mind (*cittotpāda*) are subsumed within this stage. Up to this point, all are included within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
It is called "equipment" because the two matters of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna*) cultivated in this stage provide nourishment and benefit to one's own person.
Because it serves as sustenance for the provisions [of the path], it may also be called "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*). For the sake of sentient beings, one diligently seeks liberation;
since "liberation" is a designation for *nirvāṇa*, and this practice does not contradict that goal, it is termed "conducive.
As for "part" (*bhāga*), it means cause or constituent. Because it is a cause of liberation—a single constituent of the cause—it is called a "part."
The previous [stage] was defined by self-benefit, whereas this one relies upon benefiting others; thus, although they share the same stage, their two names differ.

In this stage, because the bodhisattva relies on the causes of virtuous friends, mental attention, the provisions, and the four powers, he possesses deep faith and understanding regarding the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only);
yet, he has not yet realized the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper, and for the most part dwells in outward-directed activities while practicing the bodhisattva path.

Therefore, regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) induced by the two types of grasping, there is as yet no power capable of subduing or extinguishing them so as to prevent the manifestation of those two types of grasping.
This explains the latter two lines of the verse: although the Bodhisattva at this stage relies upon the four powers, he is unable to subdue the two types of grasping.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): that which relies on the power of causes refers to the two types of natures—the innate (*sahaja*) and that formed through habituation (*abhyāsa*).
That which relies on the power of a virtuous friend refers to the various Buddhas. As for the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it is due to its decisiveness.

This is its essential nature (*svabhāva*). It takes the grasping at a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*) as its primary element, because it gives rise to other hindrances such as views, doubt, ignorance, craving, hatred, and pride.
This explains its essential character; its enumeration is the same as that of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*).

If these are necessarily present within the afflictive hindrance, yet the afflictive hindrance is coarse and belongs to the category of what is abandoned by the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is merely this [hindrance of objects].
Because they are wholesome and obscured by nature, they are manifested by way of numerical categories. Now, the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is subtle and lacks many varieties;
it is abandoned only by Bodhisattvas, and it is also subsumed under the neutral state of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*). Therefore, its numerical categories are not explicitly displayed.

Furthermore, it is shown that the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha-avidyā*) is comprised within only one of the five levels of abiding (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), whereas the aforementioned hindrances are comprised within four of the levels of abiding. Thus [the distinction is made].

It is not explicitly enumerated. If that is so, why does it not say "all secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*)? Since it already mentions "pride and so forth," there is no fault in including the secondary afflictions by means of the term "and so forth.
Regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*): they are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena in their non-erroneous nature, namely, suchness (*tathatā*).

Because this object is obscured, wisdom fails to arise; since it can obstruct enlightenment (*bodhi*), it is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). As for the aforementioned afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

It is an obstruction; [in this case] it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). This cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstructs that which is to be known; [in this case] it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).
Therefore, the two are distinct.

This cognitive obscuration is definitely not concomitant with the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), because the latter is subtle and weak, and because it is not associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because it is associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), and because the category of knowledge regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arises simultaneously with it.

The following section analyzes this in terms of consciousness; this clarifies that the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*) lacks such grasping. This is stated in order to refute external attachments; within the eighth consciousness, such grasping certainly does not exist.
That ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) is subtle, minute, and weak, whereas this grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is coarse and necessarily strong.
It must be that which is capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*), and not that which is co-existent with it. However, Master Sthiramati maintains that there is a grasping [of phenomena];
the Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "Because it is not associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).

All treatises state that this eighth consciousness is associated only with the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), and because it is not associated with ignorance or wisdom, the grasping of phenomena (*dharmanirgraha*) must be associated with this [consciousness].

Because both [the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena and the eighth consciousness] would coexist. Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas enter the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena, it can coexist with the eighth ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

If the eighth were possessed of grasping (*sopādāna*), they could not coexist; it should be like the seventh consciousness, which does not coexist with the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena.
Among the seven evolving consciousnesses, they arise either in small or large numbers according to their respective conditions, as explained in the case of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because the five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and the others—are devoid of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpaka*), they are necessarily dissociated from views, doubt, and so forth; however, the remaining [afflictions] may all be induced through the power of the mental consciousness (*manas*).

It is clarified that the first seven consciousnesses do not arise separately from the afflictions (*kleśa*) to give rise to this grasping; therefore, the number of this grasping is identical to that of the afflictions.

If the seventh consciousness possesses four root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the wisdom of the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣayaka*), there are thirteen dharmas in total.
If the sixth consciousness possesses all of these, while the five sensory consciousnesses possess only the three root afflictions. The secondary [afflictions]...

The ten types of delusions are associated with thirteen factors, including the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). As for "without views or doubt," this is because the five sensory consciousnesses lack constructive discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Thus, the ten [afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*) are complete, while the other ten are present only in part.

Those [afflictions] produced by constructive discrimination are entirely absent from the five sensory consciousnesses; it is not that the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) are absent from them. This is what is meant by "without parts."

It is distinct. Although it lacks independent power to give rise to the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*), there is no fault in its arising because it is induced by the mental faculty (*manas*).

This hindrance is associated only with the two types of mind—unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*)—because the treatises state that ignorance (*avidyā*) pertains exclusively to the natures of unwholesomeness and neutrality, and because delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) are not mutually dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Regarding the classification by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): it is associated only with the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 59, states that for those in the higher realms, it is exclusively indeterminate; whereas in the lower realms, it extends to the unwholesome, because delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) are not mutually exclusive.
According to Sthiramati, all three natures involve grasping.

Among the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), this particular obscuration must necessarily exist, because that [affliction] definitely takes this as its basis; although their essence is not different.

However, their functions differ; thus, regarding the two types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), as they function in accordance with the Noble Path, there are superior and inferior degrees, and their abandonment may occur either sequentially or simultaneously.

This explains the difference between their breadth and narrowness. If this cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) necessarily exists within the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), then that afflictive obstruction must certainly take this [cognitive] obstruction as its basis, because the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is more extensive; the objects of the afflictions must necessarily be phenomena.
Therefore, although their essence is not different and they arise from the same seed, their functions are distinct, as they differ in their obstruction of either *nirvāṇa* or *bodhi*.

Regarding the sequence of abandonment: some first abandon the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) but do not abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), such as those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Others first abandon the cognitive obstructions but do not abandon the afflictive obstructions, as occurs on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

Regarding the states of abiding, emerging from meditation, and so forth, because the Bodhisattvas of the subsequent stages are described according to their seeds (*bīja*), there are cases where both [the afflictions and the objects] are abandoned;
for example, as with the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Alternatively, there are cases where neither is abandoned, as with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others.

Among the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states, this is that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), not the other three types. Those [other types], such as the deportment (*airyāpathika*), have weak functional power;

they do not obscure what is to be known, nor do they obstruct enlightenment. Thus it is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*), speaking from the perspective of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If viewed from the perspective of a bodhisattva, it is also "obscured" (*nivṛta*).
Although there are four types of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states, this hindrance is exclusively of the "ripening-neutral" (*vipākāvyākṛta*) variety.

The other three types of neutral states—those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so forth—are weak in their power; they do not obscure the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and thus do not hinder enlightenment (*bodhi*). If otherwise...
The innate [afflictions] are powerful and pervasive; they arise from conceptualization and can obscure the objects of knowledge, thereby obstructing bodhi.
Regarding the term "unobscured" (anivṛta), this is said in reference to the two vehicles, for they may manifest during the two stages of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
However, if viewed from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, they are indeed obscured, as they obstruct bodhi.

[The opponent] objects: "If the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) include views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth, how can this type [of obscuration] be described in the sūtras as the 'ground of the abiding of ignorance' (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*)?

Furthermore, if these obscurations also contain views and doubt, why does the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* state that the cognitive obscurations constitute the ground of the stage of non-learner (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), and not the grounds of abiding such as doubt and the rest? This is because of that...

The Sūtra speaks of five *bhūmi-sthānas*: first, the *sthāna* of abiding in one place through views; second, the *sthāna* of abiding in craving for sense-desires; third, the *sthāna* of abiding in craving for form;
fourth, the *sthāna* of abiding in craving for existence; and fifth, the *sthāna* of abiding in ignorance. The first consists solely of afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Because these are preeminent in their delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*), they are termed "one place. Since this single place is abandoned [by the path of seeing], it is called "abiding in one place through views."

The Dwelling Grounds (*vāsabhūmi*). Next are the three types of Dwelling Grounds, beginning with Desire-Attachment (*kāmarāga*). The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) consist of three categories;

they pertain generally to both the confusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and principles (*tattva*). When categorized according to the realms (*dhātu*), they are divided into three types. Each of these is abandoned through both Seeing (*darśana*) and Cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
All cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are collectively termed the "ground of the abiding of ignorance" (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).

Because they do not consist of distinct categories and because they lack specific modes of activity that are deluded regarding the various truths (*satya*), they are established as a whole under the name "ground of the abiding of ignorance. "Ground" (*bhūmi*) has the meaning of a basis;

it refers to the fact that all seeds serve as the support for the manifest [defilements], and thus it is called a "ground. This concludes the statement of the opponent's objection. Below, the Master of the Treatise provides the response.
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates, it is collectively termed "ignorance," yet this does not mean that views and the other afflictions are absent.

This is just as the seeds of the afflictions are established under the single heading of "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), or as the four stages of abiding (*catvāra āśraya-bhūmayaḥ*) are designated by the names of craving for desire, form, and existence (*kāma-rūpa-bhava-tṛṣṇā*). How could it be that those [stages] lack pride (*māna*), ignorance, and so forth?

Because ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is designated by the name "ignorance. This does not mean that other afflictions (*kleśa*), such as views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are absent.
Regarding the phrase "ignorance predominates": it is called predominant because it is deluded regarding all objects and obstructs all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, while the seeds of the afflictions exist in both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), those that arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) are designated by the single term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); how could one possibly divide them?

Within the category of "separate," there are no further afflictions such as greed; within the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), only craving for the desire realm (*kāmarāga*) and craving for existence in the form realm (*rūpabhavarāga*) are mentioned.

Does this mean that afflictions such as hatred (*dveṣa*) do not exist there? However, at the beginning [of the path of seeing] one only perceives [the objects], while later [on the path of cultivation] one speaks only of craving. Since these are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), [they are not included].

Because the power of views (*dṛṣṭi*) predominates, they are primarily characterized by conceptual discrimination; therefore, they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Because the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) predominates, it is the delusion that moistens rebirth;

therefore, it is the "ground of abiding in the attachment to dharmas" (*dharmagrāhāvasthāna-bhūmi*). Because the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates, it is called "ignorance"; this does not mean that the others are absent.

Regarding these two obstructions: those that arise through conceptual discrimination are subsumed under what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*); those that arise spontaneously are subsumed under what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The followers of the two vehicles can only abandon the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas Bodhisattvas abandon both; the permanent abandonment of these two types is possible only through the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
The suppression of the two types of active defilements (*samudācāra*) pertains generally to the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*);

the abandonment of these two may be understood accordingly. As for the distinction according to the individual: the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) are only able to abandon the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because they seek *nirvāṇa*.

They do not abandon the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Bodhisattvas abandon both, because they obstruct the two fruits [of Buddhahood]. If one suppresses the afflictions through the path with outflows...

Because at the time of affliction (*kleśa*), the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) that accompanies it also does not arise, this is called "suppressing the grasping at phenomena. It is not that a separate path arises to suppress it;
rather, if it were the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), it would necessarily eradicate the seeds.

While the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), although the two types of coarse manifest activities (*paryavasthāna*) have been suppressed, regarding the subtle ones and the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), their power of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is weak; thus, they are not yet able to suppress or extinguish them.
In this stage, the coarse aspects of the two obstacles may be suppressed;

however, as for the influence of false teachers and false teachings, if one examines them through personal reflection, the subtle afflictions of conceptual discrimination and the seeds of both [obstacles] cannot yet be suppressed or extinguished due to the weakness of the power of concentration and wisdom.
Having concluded the explanation of the verse above, the following explains the name of the stage.

In this stage, one has not yet realized the suchness of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra-tathatā*). Relying on the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one cultivates various superior practices;

it should be understood that this is also subsumed within the Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). This explains the stages. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* subsumes these five stages into four grounds, namely: Resolute Conviction...

The stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) consists of the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the term "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*), it carries the meaning of determination. It is the mental engagement of conceptual understanding (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*) through determination by means of a distracted mind;
because one has not yet realized direct realization, this is also called the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the characteristics of the sublime practices one cultivates, how are they defined?
The following explains the practice of cultivation.
This question is briefly twofold: for the sake of merit and for the sake of wisdom. Among all sublime practices, those whose nature is discernment (*prajñā*) are all termed "wisdom."
The remainder is called merit (*puṇya*).
This clarifies the two types of practice: merit and wisdom (*jñāna*). This is the general text.
Furthermore, based on the six *pāramitās*, their common characteristics are both twofold; as for their specific characteristics, the first five are described as merit.
The sixth is wisdom (*prajñā*). Alternatively, the first three are comprised solely of merit (*puṇya*), while the last one is solely wisdom.
The remaining ones pertain to both types. Regarding their common characteristic, those that function together with wisdom and assist in the accomplishment of wisdom are all termed "wisdom.

Those that arise simultaneously with merit and clarify the accomplishment of merit are all termed "merit. This is an exposition of their essential nature based on their associated companions; as for their definitive intrinsic nature:
Regarding their nature: the first five are called merit (*puṇya*), because they are not of the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*); the last one is wisdom, because it is not of the nature of merit.
Alternatively, the first three may be designated as merit alone, because they are remote from wisdom; the last one is wisdom alone, because its essential nature is discernment (*prajñā*).
Vigor and meditative concentration encompass both merit and wisdom. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 78, states:
"If one relies on vigor to practice giving and so forth, it is called merit; if one relies on vigor to cultivate the three types of wisdom and so forth, it is called wisdom."

If one cultivates the four immeasurables based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is called merit (*puṇya*); if one cultivates the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth based on meditative concentration, it is called knowledge (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, there are two kinds of sublime practices cultivated for the benefit of oneself and others; all of these are universally applicable according to the power of one's resolute intention (*āśaya*).

The practices for the benefit of oneself and others are explained according to their specific characteristics: the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth, are subsumed under the practice for one's own benefit;
the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, are all subsumed under the practice for the benefit of others. Such practices as these...
The distinctions are boundless; all are the sublime practices cultivated herein, namely the two types of beneficial conduct.

In their general characteristics, they all apply universally. As for their specific characteristics: the six perfections, the factors of enlightenment, and the uncommon marks and signs are all termed self-benefit.
The four means of integration—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—are [the means of benefiting others].
The immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—are all practices for the benefit of others.
These various dharmas are the sublime practices cultivated in this stage.
Although the two obscurations have not yet been subdued or eliminated at this stage, when practicing the sublime conduct, one may experience three types of despondency;
nevertheless, by refining the mind through such activities, one remains courageous and does not retreat from what is to be realized and cultivated.
The following explains "refining and polishing" (*parikarma*). "Refining" (*pari*) means tempering; "polishing" (*karma*) means grinding to a luster. This is the general statement.
First, upon hearing that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is vast, profound, and far-reaching, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
One then refines and polishes one's own mind by citing others who have realized great enlightenment, thereby becoming courageous and non-retrogressive.
Regarding "the first bodhicitta is vast, extensive, deep, and far-reaching": "vast" means boundless; "extensive" means unsurpassed;
"deep" means difficult to fathom; and "far-reaching" means long in duration. For these reasons, one may consequently become discouraged and should be encouraged by citing others as examples.
Those who have already realized great enlightenment undergo such refinement. [Thinking: "Ordinary beings cultivate practice and realize the fruit;
I am of the same class as they. Why should I regress? Thus, the verse of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, all sentient beings aspire to realize the fruit of the Sugata. Since they are great men, so too am I; one should not disparage oneself and regress."
[The term] *kuñcita* (contracted) is explained at length as in other commentaries.
Second, when one hears that the perfections such as generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) are extremely difficult to practice, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
By reflecting that one’s own disposition is capable of practicing generosity and the like, one refines one's own mind, becoming courageous and non-retrogressive.
Second, regarding the difficulty of practicing the ten thousand deeds and succumbing to discouragement: one should reflect upon oneself and increase one's cultivation through refinement.

If, upon hearing of giving and the other perfections, the mind feels discouraged, one should examine oneself and practice them gradually. By tempering and training the mind in this way, one will no longer succumb to discouragement.
Third, upon hearing that the perfect transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to realize, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
By citing the coarse virtues of others—let alone one’s own sublime causes—one refines one's own mind so as to be courageous and non-retrogressive. Through these three matters, one refines the mind.
Firm and ardent, one cultivates all supreme practices.
Regarding the third transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is difficult to realize, one may feel discouraged; therefore, one should use coarse examples to illustrate the subtle.

If, upon hearing that the transformation of the basis into the fruit of Buddhahood is difficult to realize, one becomes despondent and withdraws, one should point to the coarse virtues of others—such as the practice of giving—which even result in noble status and happiness; how much more so for me?

Is there no fruit for the pure and sublime goodness one cultivates? It is because the bodhisattva undergoes these three kinds of refinement that they cultivate superior practices without falling into despondency or retreat.
Next, regarding the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): what are its characteristics?
This question arises to explain the second stage, the stage of application.
The verse says:
To manifestly posit a slight object and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only— because there is something apprehended—
one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.
This is the response given in verse.

The treatise says: Having first, during the initial incalculable eon, well-cultivated the provisions of merit and wisdom, and having brought the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) to completion, the bodhisattva further cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) in order to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and abide in the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), thereby subduing and eliminating the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).

These four—namely, Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*)—are collectively termed the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). They lead toward...

Because they constitute the stage of "True Determination" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and because they are proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are designated by the name "Preparatory Effort" (*prayoga*). This does not imply that the preceding Stage of Requisites (*sambhāra*) lacks the sense of preparatory effort.

[This] clarifies the basis for these stages and lists their names. These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) belong to both [the first and second dhyānas] and are cultivated at the final moment of the first *kalpa*.

Therefore, it is said that previously, during the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), in order to cultivate the provisions of merit and wisdom, one fulfills the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

Desiring to advance to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and to suppress and eliminate the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), one cultivates the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*): namely, heat (*uṣmagata*), summit (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

These four are collectively termed the "factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). They are so called because they lead toward and accord with the definitive discernment (*nirvedha*) of reality.

"Decisive discernment" (*nirvedha*) is wisdom; it is precisely the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). "Decisive" (*nir*) signifies "resolution," thus it is called the "stage of decisive discernment" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

"Decisive" excludes the category of doubt (*vicikitsā*), for that is characterized by hesitation. "Discernment" (*pravicaya*) excludes the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*), for that does not involve discernment. While the category of doubt involves discernment, it lacks decisiveness.

Because the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is decisive yet not analytical, this stage of knowledge is called the "Stage of Decisive Discrimination" (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). "Stage" (*bhāga*) has the meaning of a "limb" (*aṅga*) or a "portion.

It refers specifically to the limb of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*), which exists within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Because this is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "real" (*tattva*);

because that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) is not real, [the former] is so designated. These four—Heat (*uṣmagata*) and the others—which accord with and lead toward that [path of seeing], are called "conducive to decisive discrimination" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

This portion is still close to the Path of Seeing and is therefore still called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*); it is not the preceding stage of "provisioning" (*sambhāra*), as that lacks the meaning of "application.
This is to show that the preceding stage of the provisioning path is also designated as "application."

The four dharmas, beginning with "warming" (*ūṣmagata*), are established according to the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four cognitions of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*). These are established in their initial and final stages.

The four thorough investigations consist of investigating names (*nāman*), objects (*artha*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*)—understanding them through thorough knowledge as being conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent, and realizing that these four are devoid of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
And the non-existence of consciousness is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

The following explains the stages (*avasthā*): the first two stages involve the contemplation of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*), while the latter two involve the contemplation of true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*). Therefore, they are referred to as the "initial and final stages.
Regarding the establishment of the four thorough investigations: first is the thorough investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*); second is the thorough investigation of objects (*artha-paryeṣaṇā*).

Third, one investigates the names, objects, and intrinsic natures; fourth, one investigates the distinctions between names and objects. One investigates these four because they all exist only as designations (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the four types of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*): through the preceding four investigations, one contemplates that the four objects grasped by the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are separate from consciousness and do not exist.

This is because one has only contemplated the non-existence of the apprehended (*grāhya*), but has not yet contemplated the apprehending (*grāhaka*). This knowledge of reality is the stage of "acceptance" (*kṣānti*) regarding what was previously [contemplated].

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): once it is realized that it does not exist apart from consciousness and that the apprehended (*grāhya*) is empty, one further thoroughly understands that the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), which is that consciousness, is also definitely non-existent apart from the internal object.
Thus, the apprehending subject is also empty. One realizes that internal consciousness and its transformed appearances are mutually inseparable, like magical illusions and the like;
this is called the wisdom that knows reality (*tattvajñāna*). Question: For what reason are the phenomena (*dharma*) and their names and meanings [distinct]?
One seeks them separately regarding the intrinsic nature and the specific differences of name and object;
one examines them together because the characteristics of name and object are distinct, yet one contemplates them as a pair because their respective characteristics are identical.
This refers to two kinds: name and meaning. First, sameness of intrinsic nature; second, sameness of differentiation.
Therefore, by combining the two kinds—name and meaning—and their two respective intrinsic natures and differentiations, they are unified as the object of contemplation.

Based on the *ālokalabdha-samādhi*, one gives rise to inferior investigation (*vitarka*) and contemplates the non-existence of the apprehended object (*grāhya*); this is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

This means that within this stage, one first contemplates that the four factors—the name and so forth—which constitute the apprehended object, are all transformations of one's own mind; they are merely provisionally designated and have no substantial reality that can be found.

Because it is the precursor to the sun of wisdom first being attained, it is established as "clarity" (*āloka*) and receives that name. Since this is also the precursor to the fire of the Path that is about to be attained, it is also called "heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Clarity is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while analytical reflection is wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it is termed "arising. It observes only the grasped object; thus, there are four [aspects]: name, meaning, and so forth.
All phenomena are merely transformations of one's own mind and are ultimately unattainable. Because one has obtained the sun of wisdom, this stage is designated "Attainment of Clarity" (mṛdumūrdhā).
As it is the precursor to the fire of the Path, it receives the name "Heat" (uṣmagata); this is the first stage.
Relying on the *vṛddhāloka* concentration, one gives rise to superior investigation and contemplates that there is nothing to be grasped; this is established as the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

That is to say, within this stage, one repeatedly contemplates that the four dharmas—name and so forth—which constitute the object of apprehension, are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations and being ultimately unobtainable in reality.

Because the signs of light (*āloka-nimitta*) become increasingly intense, it is called "Increasing Light" (*ālokavṛddhi*). Because it represents the culmination of the stage of investigation (*vitarka*), it is further named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

The preceding "Attainment of Light" (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*) relies on lower-level investigation, whereas this "Increasing Light" (*ālokavṛddhi-samādhi*) relies on higher-level investigation. "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) carries the meaning of "culmination.
"Increasing" (*vṛddhi*) refers to becoming more intense. The remainder of the text is easy to understand. This is the second stage.

Relying on the seal of conformity (*anulomika-nidhyapti*), one gives rise to the lower stage of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). One definitively seals and maintains the state of the non-apprehended (*an-upādāna*);

within the absence of the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), one likewise conforms to and accepts this with patience (*kṣānti*). Since there is no real object (*viṣaya*), apart from the apprehending consciousness (*vijñāna*), how could there be a real consciousness?

Because the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject are established in mutual dependence, at the time of sealing and conforming through patience, it is collectively designated as "patience" (*kṣānti*), which seals what preceded and conforms to it.
Subsequently, it is established as "seal" (*mudrā*) and "conformity" (*anuloma*). Because the consciousness that perceives the object is empty, it is also called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

It is a "seal" because it confirms that the previously grasped object does not exist; it is "conformity" because it conforms to the subsequent non-existence of the grasper. This serves to confirm the certainty [attained] at the preceding stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Within the state of non-apprehension, one definitively seals and maintains it; therein lies superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Within the state of non-apprehension of the grasper (*grāhaka*), there is likewise the patience of conforming to joy (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Now, within this patience, there are generally three grades. Patience of the inferior grade is called "sealing patience" (*mudrā-kṣānti*), because it seals the non-existence of the apprehended (*grāhya*).
If it is of the middle grade, it is called "joyful conformity," because one joyfully conforms to the non-existence of the grasper and practices accordingly.

If the superior grade of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) is designated merely as "seal and conformity" (*mudrā-anuloma*), it is because the seal (*mudrā*) is able to grasp non-existence, while conformity (*anuloma*) contemplates that [non-existence].

Therefore, these three grades of patience are combined and termed "the concentration of seal and conformity" (*mudrā-anuloma-samādhi*). Patience (*kṣānti*) is wisdom (*jñāna*); when this wisdom is conjoined with the seal and conformity, it is called the "concentration of seal and conformity.

Since object and consciousness are mutually dependent, if the object is non-existent, how could the essence of consciousness exist? Thus, the patience of seal and conformity is collectively termed simply "patience."

Regarding "Seal and Accordance" (Yinshun): it is called "Seal and Accordance" because it seals the non-existence of the previously grasped object and accords with the subsequent non-existence of the grasper.
These three grades of patience—patience regarding the object and patience regarding consciousness—are all entirely empty; therefore, they are collectively termed "patience. This is the third stage.

Relying on the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the superior knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which seals the emptiness of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*). This establishes the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

That is to say, while the preceding stage of "Superior Patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) seals only the emptiness of the grasper (*grāhaka*), the present Supreme Mundane Dharma seals both forms of emptiness simultaneously. Immediately following this, [the Path of Seeing arises].

One will necessarily enter the path of seeing; therefore, it is designated by the name "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). Because this is the most supreme among the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is termed "uninterrupted" because it is immediately adjacent to the path of seeing. Within the state of an ordinary being, both the grasper and the grasped are sealed as empty.
The "Victorious" (jaya) is named the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), which is the fourth stage.

In this manner, through the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan), one contemplates the emptiness of the apprehended object based upon the apprehending consciousness. Upon the arising of the lower degree of Patience (kṣānti), one awaits and seals the characteristic of the emptiness of the object.

At the stage of the transition of medium patience, one accords with and accepts that the grasping consciousness is empty, just as its objects are; at the stage of the arising of superior patience, one seals the emptiness of the grasper;
and at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas, one seals both aspects of emptiness.

This is a general explanation of the higher stages. The stages of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit) may be understood accordingly. However, within the three types of *kṣānti* (Patience), regarding the middle stage of the middle *kṣānti*:

"conforming to the acceptance of pleasure" (*sukha-kṣamaṇa-anuloma*) refers to conforming to the subsequent stage, which is the highest degree of *kṣānti*. "Conforming to the absence of a grasper" (*grāhaka-abhāva-anuloma*) refers to the same. The remainder of the text is easy to understand.

Because they all still possess signs, they have not yet realized the truth. Therefore, it is said that within these four stages, the Bodhisattva still establishes a slight object before them, asserting it to be the true ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). This is because the two signs of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated.

Because one perceives the mind while retaining its phenomenal marks (*sanimitta*), one does not truly abide in the principle of true *vijñapti-mātratā*. Only after those marks have ceased does one truly abide [in that principle].
This explains the verse. When the mind transforms into an appearance, it is called a "slight object" (*alpavastu*); because this is not without marks, it is termed "retaining marks."

When these marks are realized as true, they are extinguished. These "marks" refer to the marks of what is grasped as empty, the marks of the dependent nature, and what is called the mark of the existence of emptiness—that is, the mark of emptiness existing within [the dependent].
This is the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of that very consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Because of the presence of these marks, one has not yet realized the truth; it is only by extinguishing the mark of the existence of emptiness that one realizes the truth.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:

When the Bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, He contemplates that the reflected image is nothing but mind. Once the conceptualization of objects has been eliminated, He scrutinizes that it is merely his own perception;
Thus abiding in the internal mind, He knows that the apprehended object does not exist.
"Next, the grasper is also non-existent; finally, contact is subsumed under non-apprehension.
This is a verse from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. "The Bodhisattva, in the state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-avasthā*)" indicates that this is not the state of distraction.

"Observing that the reflection is merely mind" means observing the internal mental object (*ālambana*), which does not exist apart from the mind; this occurs during the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Once conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) has ceased, [the stage of] "Investigation" (*vicāra*) is eliminated.

Regarding "contemplating that there are only one's own perceptions": this refers to the state where there is only the internal mind; this occurs at the stage of the Peak (*mūrdhan*). Thus far, these constitute the two stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and the Peak.
The two phrases, "abiding thus in the internal mind" and "knowing that the apprehended object does not exist," correspond to the stage of Lower Patience (*kṣānti*).

Next, "the apprehending subject is also non-existent" corresponds to the stages of Middle and Upper Patience. Taken together, these three levels of Patience confirm both types of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*); this is the first [moment] of the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Regarding this single dharma: because the time is short, it is explained from the perspective of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Subsequently, one touches upon non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), which is the stage of the path (*mārga*).

In this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) has not yet been dispelled, nor has the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) been severed; one can only suppress and eliminate them.
The conceptualization of the two grasps contradicts the path of seeing;

therefore, regarding the innate [grasps] and their two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), because the mind of impure contemplation still possesses apprehension and conceptualization, they have not been entirely subdued or eliminated.
What is called "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*) refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), which binds the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and so forth.

"Bondage by coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) refers to the outflows, latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and so on. At this stage, the Bodhisattva has not yet severed these two bondages;

he is only able to suppress and eliminate the dualistic grasping of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-dvaya-grāha*), because that dualistic grasping contradicts the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). As for innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*) and its two seeds, [he cannot yet eliminate them].
They have not yet been eliminated, nor has the untainted state (*anāsrava*) been attained, because there is still grasping at objects and because there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

At this stage, the bodhisattva practices the observation of both the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) and the non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*), in order to induce the two types of vision in the future and to suppress the two types of obstacles consisting of conceptual discrimination. Among these, the non-established truth is the primary object of observation.
It is not like the two vehicles, which observe only the established [truth].
As the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "There are two sets of the four noble truths: the conditioned and the unconditioned. The unconditioned noble truth is the non-established [truth].
That which possesses differentiated names and expressions is called 'established'; that which is undifferentiated and free from names and expressions is called..."
It is not established. "Established" means that which is conceptually designated (*prajñapti*).

In this stage, if the Bodhisattva does not perform the non-dual contemplation, they cannot induce the vision of the true nature of those [dharmas], because two kinds of births would arise; nor can they subdue the followers of the Two Vehicles.
However, it is not the case that what is being correctly observed is not established [in its specific nature].

When a bodhisattva gives rise to these roots of virtue, such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, although they may pertain to any of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) during the stage of skillful means, they rely specifically upon the fourth concentration.

Only then is it fully accomplished, for by relying on the most excellent support, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). It arises solely based on a body within the happy realms (*sugati*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because other types of wisdom or aversion of mind are not particularly distinguished.
When first cultivating the four roots of goodness, such as *ūṣmagata*, one may rely on any of the preceding dhyānas.

However, at the stage of completion, one must rely on the fourth dhyāna, because one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by depending on the most excellent basis. Nevertheless, the physical body that serves as the support must belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This is because the bodies of the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*)—which are bodies of the happy migrations (*sugati*)—do not possess the kind of revulsion toward existence that is required. Furthermore, the bodies of the miserable migrations (*durgati*) within the desire realm...
This is because their wisdom-mind is not particularly superior. The *Ṣoḍaśākāra-śāstra* (Sixteen Verses) states: "Extreme grief does not occur in the evil destinies;
extreme joy does not occur in the two higher realms. It occurs only among humans and gods of the desire realm when a Buddha appears in the world and they attain direct realization (*abhisamaya*)."

This stage is also called being subsumed under the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), because one has not yet realized the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
According to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, it is included within the fourth stage; this stage is also called being subsumed under the Stage of Practice through Understanding.
Next is the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*). What are its six characteristics?
This question arises to explain the third stage, the stage of thorough penetration.
The verse says:
"When at that time, regarding the object of cognition, wisdom finds nothing whatsoever to be apprehended— then one abides in mere consciousness (vijñapti-mātra),
because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings.
Thus he answers with this verse.

The treatise says: When a bodhisattva, regarding the objects of focus, possesses non-conceptual wisdom that attains nothing at all—because it does not grasp the various marks of conceptual proliferation—at that time, one is said to truly abide in the true ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). This is the realization of *tathatā* (suchness).
Wisdom and *tathatā* are equal and identical, for both are free from the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). The grasper and...

Grasping at signs is in every case conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), for it manifests as the proliferation of discursive thought (*prapañca*) based on the mind that perceives something to be attained.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the verse. At this time, when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, there is absolutely nothing attained because no signs are grasped.
"Not grasping" means the absence of the grasping subject (*grāhaka*). Regarding "the signs of proliferation," there is no... [object].
Grasping at signs and contemplating the true ultimate reality is called "non-apprehension. At that time, one is said to truly abide in *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
Both the realizing wisdom and the realized *tathatā* (suchness) are devoid of the two-fold grasping; therefore, they are called "equality.
Since those two forms of grasping arise from the conceptualizing mind, and this state is non-conceptual, it is the equality of non-duality.
There is an interpretation that this wisdom lacks both parts, because it is said to be devoid of the characteristics of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka).
Regarding the explanation of these two parts, there are three distinct masters. This first master also maintains that both parts are absent;
for the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that within this category of wisdom, the two types of grasping do not exist.

One interpretation holds that this wisdom possesses both the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*). It is called "taking that as its object" because it arises bearing the image of that [object].
The second master says: Both parts exist together. Because it arises bearing the image of that [object], there is an image-part which is named "taking that as its object";
therefore, there is also a seeing-part. This is the statement of his thesis.
If that which lacks the aspect [of the object] were called "that which takes it as its object," then the cognition of form and so forth would have to be called the cognition of sound and so forth.

If there were no seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it would be incapable of taking an object; how then could it be said to be the cognition that takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its object? Let it not be the case that the nature of *tathatā* itself is also a cognizing subject.
Therefore, one must admit this [existence of] the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of meditative concentration;
this refutes the former master. To refute the absence of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it is said:

"If that which lacks an image resembling the object were called 'that which perceives it,' then the cognitions of color and so forth would have to be named after this sound and so forth. This is because within these cognitions of color and so forth, there is no image of sound and so forth. Thus he refutes [the opponent].

The "No-View" [proponent] says: If there were no viewing portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it would be unable to take an object. As previously stated, this wisdom is called "wisdom that takes suchness as its object," or it has the nature of true cognition;
therefore, it must be capable of taking an object. Thus, one must admit the existence of the viewing portion, because it is that which is capable of taking an object.
There is an interpretation that this wisdom perceives the existence of marks and yet is said to be "without marks" because it does not grasp at marks.

Although it possesses a seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it is without conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and is thus said to be "not a grasper" (*an-upādātṛ*); however, this does not mean that grasping is entirely absent.

The third master says: "There is seeing but no aspect. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states that this "aspectless apprehension" (*animitta-grahaṇa*) within the category of wisdom is called "aspectless apprehension" because it does not apprehend aspects.
Although it possesses a seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it lacks conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); therefore, it is said to be "without apprehension.
This does not mean that the part itself is non-existent. Since there is no aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), how can it be called "taking that as its object"?
Although there is no objective aspect (nimittabhāga), it can be said that this [consciousness] arises bearing the semblance of suchness, because it is not separate from suchness.

Just as the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) perceives the seeing aspect (darśanabhāga) without undergoing transformation, this [consciousness] should likewise be so. If it were to perceive through transformation, it would not be a direct realization.

Just as with subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it must possess conceptualization; therefore, one should admit that this [wisdom] has vision (*darśana*) but lacks mental images (*nimitta*).

This wisdom that takes reality as its object arises by carrying the essential nature and characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) along with it, and is thus called "having suchness as its object" (*ālambana*).

It does not arise by carrying a reflected image (*pratibimba*) as a distinct objective part (*ākāra-bhāga*); rather, because it is inseparable from suchness, it is said to take suchness as its object. To clarify this through an analogy, it is like self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Regarding the divisions [of consciousness], when the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes [an object] as its condition, it does not bear the image (*nimitta*) of that object, because it is designated as the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This non-conceptual [wisdom] differs from the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); therefore, it must be without images. If it possessed images, it would be identical to the subsequently attained wisdom, which is not a direct realization (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*).

Immediately following the preparatory application, when this wisdom arises, one realizes and experiences true knowledge; this is called the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*). Because it is the first illumination of the principle, it is also called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The term "śikṣā" (釋) refers to its designation. From the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises without further interval;

this is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). "Seeing" (*darśana*) is itself the path (*mārga*). "Essence" (*tattva*) means penetration; "realization" (*saṃgama*) means thorough attainment. Illuminating the principle is termed "seeing"; its meaning is easy to understand.

However, this path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), briefly stated, is of two kinds. First is the true path of vision (*tattva-darśana-mārga*), which refers to the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
It truly realizes the ultimate truth revealed by the two emptinesses and truly severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) regarding conceptualization.
Although many moments (*kṣaṇa*) are required for the matter to reach its consummation, because they are equal in nature, it is collectively described as a single mind.
The following explains the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) through two types of distinctions: first, the true (*tattva*); second, the phenomenal (*nimitta*).

Regarding the true Path of Seeing, its essence consists precisely of fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which directly realizes the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) and truly abandons the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

Regarding "although there are many moments": if one sees the path with a single mind, the combination of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and a single path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is termed "many moments," yet these are collectively designated as "one mind.
It is not that there are multiple mental instants within the uninterrupted path itself.
There is one interpretation that within this context, the two emptinesses and the two obstacles are realized and abandoned progressively, because there are differences of depth and coarseness.

There are two masters who offer this explanation; this is the first master’s view. The two emptinesses are realized progressively and the two obstacles are abandoned progressively, because according to principle there are levels of depth and because the obstacles have degrees of coarseness; thus they are realized and abandoned gradually.

One interpretation holds that herein the two emptinesses and the two obstructions are realized and severed simultaneously; this is because, through the power of the aspirational intention (*āśaya*), one possesses such capability.
A second master states that the two emptinesses are realized simultaneously and the two obstructions are severed simultaneously;

since both were already severed by the aspirational intention during the preceding stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), they do not function as three distinct stages upon entering the state of meditative observation (*darśana-mārga*). Thus, it is known that there is necessarily no sequence between severance and realization.

Second is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). This, in turn, has two aspects. First is the contemplation of the non-established truths (*avyavasthāpita-satya*), which consists of three grades of mind:
1. The wisdom that internally eliminates the conceptual designation of sentient beings (*sattva-prajñapti*); it can eliminate the weak-grade latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of discrimination. 2.

The wisdom that internally eliminates the conceptual designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*); it can eliminate the medium-grade latent tendencies of discrimination. 3. The wisdom that universally eliminates the conceptual designations of all sentient beings and all phenomena.

Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is able to eliminate all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptual discrimination. The first two are called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-jñāna*) because they each take their objects individually;
the third is called "subsequent knowledge" because it takes its objects collectively.

This explains the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) characterized by the three mental states. Regarding "the non-established" (*apratiṣṭhita*): this refers to *tathatā* (suchness), as previously explained. Regarding "internal elimination":

this means that one eliminates the conventional (*prajñapti*) by taking only the internal body as the object. Regarding the "conventionality of sentient beings" (*sattva-prajñapti*): first, one conceives of sentient beings;

these are all falsely conceived, existing only because they appear as sentient beings due to the mind. To speak of their lack of intrinsic nature is called [the elimination of the conventionality of sentient beings].

"Of the conventional" refers to the wisdom that takes conditions as its object; this means the cognizing mind itself takes the internal body as its object. This is the wisdom that eliminates the conventionality of a sentient being.
The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. Now, in this context, the two obstacles—of persons and phenomena—are each divided into upper and lower levels.

The coarse is superior; the subtle is inferior. Together they form four categories. However, the two coarse [levels] are each eliminated separately because wisdom is still weak and has not yet severed both simultaneously.
Only when superior wisdom is attained can one sever both simultaneously. This is described according to the wisdom as "weak" (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
"Weak" means inferior. The initial wisdom is called weak; the subsequent wisdom is called middling; the superior [wisdom] is called strong.

Because the former is inferior, the subsequent wisdom is called "superior. Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), this wisdom is supreme. However, the first two types of wisdom have not yet attained such excellence;
they specifically take the internal body as their object, excluding the provisional designations of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-prajñapti*). The third mind abandons [these];

its wisdom is of the highest grade (*adhimātra*) and takes both the internal and external extensively as its objects, whether as self or as phenomena. Therefore, these three are distinct. The first two are distinguished by their specific objects of focus; hence [the distinction].

Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*). The latter, which takes all [truths] as its object collectively, is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), because it follows the pattern of the former knowledge.

Regarding the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*) establish the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths separately and collectively for the specific obstacles to be abandoned by each.

This is called the Path of Vision of Names and Characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*). "Dharma" refers to the principle (*dharmatā*); its meaning is "letting go" (*prahāṇa*). Within the Path of True Vision (*tattva-darśanamārga*), there are two aspects of vision regarding the two emptinesses.

Although there is also self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), it is not considered a "dharma," because that which directly perceives suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely what constitutes "letting go. This is established from the perspective of the aspect of vision (*darśana-bhāga*).
There are uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). According to the specific obstacles abandoned by each, there are four aspects of vision (*darśana-bhāga*).

Within the uninterrupted paths, because the two aspects of vision regarding persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are distinct dharmas, there are the first two moments of mind. Within the paths of liberation, because the two aspects of vision regarding persons and phenomena are comprehensive dharmas, there is the first [remaining] moment of mind.
This is to manifest that the uninterrupted path abandons [the obstacles] either individually or collectively; therefore, they are distinguished.
It is the Dharma. Because the realization of the principle is identical, it reveals the path of liberation; therefore, they are subsumed as a whole. Thus, the treatise states:
"Established both individually and collectively, it is called the Path of Vision (darśanamārga) in terms of its names and characteristics."

One interpretation holds that these three constitute the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the path of seeing with aspects (*sākāra-darśanamārga*) takes the four noble truths as its object.
Another interpretation holds that these three constitute the path of seeing with aspects, because the true path of seeing does not take [the truths] as distinct objects.

There are two masters who offer explanations. The first master says: "These three grades of mind constitute the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), because the path of vision of images (*nimitta-darśana-mārga*) does not produce these three minds, as it takes the four truths as its object in a general way. The second master says: "This is the path of vision of images;
since the true path of vision only takes [the truths] in a general manner, how could it take them specifically as three distinct grades?"
Regarding the two types of path of insight (*darśanamārga*) based on the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*), there are sixteen moments of mind. This further consists of two parts;
the latter clarifies the characteristics of these sixteen moments. Herein, the first part provides the heading: "The path of insight has two [types]."

First, based on the observation of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), sixteen distinct types of mind are established as dharmas and categories. Specifically, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are four types of mind: 1.

**Dharma-knowledge-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):** This refers to the contemplation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Truth of Suffering within the three realms, whereby one correctly abandons the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
2. **Dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*):** This refers to the [subsequent] knowledge of that patience... [text fragment ends].
Immediately thereafter, one contemplates the previously realized *tathatā* (suchness) and realizes liberation from the previously abandoned afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is the *duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering), which refers to the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) immediately following that [receptivity], wherein one internally and individually realizes both the receptivity and the knowledge regarding the [truth of] phenomena. It is said that all subsequent noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are of this same category.

Fourth is the *duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge of suffering), which refers to the arising of untainted knowledge immediately following this [receptivity], whereby one definitively ascertains and confirms it as suffering.

Regarding the patience of wisdom (*jñāna-kṣānti*): just as there are four types of mind with respect to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it should be understood that the same applies to the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.
These sixteen minds consist of eight that contemplate suchness (*tathatā*) and eight that contemplate correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

That which is called the "apprehended" (grāhya) refers to the principle of the truths (*satya*). That which is called the "apprehender" (grāhaka) refers to the wisdom that takes that principle as its object.

The Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) take the principle as their objective domain and contemplate the apprehended. The Subsequent Patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) take the preceding category of knowledge as their object and contemplate the apprehender.
Among the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering, the first—Dharma-patience regarding the knowledge of suffering—refers to "suffering" as the Truth of Suffering and "Dharma" as...

That realization of the teaching on the Truth of Suffering is the activity of the wise. Within the Path of Preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), there is the knowledge that takes the phenomena of suffering as its object;
this "patience" (*kṣānti*) is untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*). Prior to this patience is the Knowledge of Phenomena regarding Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

This Patience of the Knowledge of Phenomena regarding Suffering, observing the lower [realm] as suffering, knows and is able to sever the twenty-eight types of proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with conceptualization within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) across the three realms: ten in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and [eight each in] the two upper realms.

The suffering of the realms (*dhātu-duḥkha*). Each [type] of suffering has nine [subdivisions], excluding the true nature (*tathatā*). Thus, across the three realms, there are twenty-eight [instances].
Regarding the second, the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*):
this refers to the dharma. (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle 17)
It is said that this commentary relies upon an ancient manuscript of the Imperial collection; it is truly a rare treasure of the age.

Within the text, essential passages from the *Jutsuki* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra) are excerpted and supplemented with further explanations, such that no trace of obscurity or difficulty remains.
Indeed, were it not for one who had inherited the dharma-garment and bowl of Great Master Ki, how could such a work have been achieved? Yet, the author remains unknown—a matter of some regret.

Is this not perhaps the incomplete twenty-fascicle commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* by Chongjun, which is recorded in the two catalogs of the various schools' commentaries transmitted from the Eastern Regions?
Its prose style closely resembles the *Fahua xuanyi zan jueze*. Furthermore, regarding the passage below the explanation of the "three kinds of despondency," it states:
"As explained at length in other commentaries," which seems to defer to what is elucidated in the *Jueze*. Herein...
At the request of the compilers of the *Zokuzōkyō*, I have briefly recorded these private views.
I await the corrections of future scholars.
July, the 42nd year of Meiji (1909). Saeki Teiin, Nanto Hōryū Gakumonji.
